title: LangGraph: StateGraph, state, reducers, edges
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: State schemas and reducers, nodes, edges and conditional edges, Command-based routing, and a router between a tool path and a text-to-SQL path.
source: LangGraph docs (docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph, langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph); LangGraph v1 release notes and migration guide; verified by running langgraph 1.2

questions.prompt: State is count: Annotated[int, operator.add] starting at 0. START fans out to nodes A and B in parallel; A returns {'count': 2} and B returns {'count': 3}. Both feed node C, which returns {'count': 1}. What is count when the graph finishes?
questions.explanation: A and B run in the same superstep and the add reducer combines both writes: 0 + 2 + 3 = 5. Then C adds 1 = 6. I ran this graph and got 6. Without the reducer the two parallel writes would raise InvalidUpdateError.

questions.prompt: An agent graph has START -> agent, a conditional edge from agent to tools (if the model requested tools) or END, and an edge tools -> agent. The model requests tools twice and then answers in plain text. How many node executions happen in total?
questions.explanation: agent, tools, agent, tools, agent = 5 executions: 3 agent runs (3 LLM calls) and 2 tool runs. I ran an equivalent graph and it produced exactly that sequence. This is the count to compare against recursion_limit.

questions.prompt: existing = [Human(id='1'), AI(id='2', content='b')]; update = [AI(id='2', content='b2'), Human(no id)]. After add_messages(existing, update), how many messages are in the list?
questions.explanation: add_messages merges by id: the update with id '2' replaces the existing message, and the message without an id gets a new generated id and is appended. 2 original (one replaced) + 1 new = 3. I verified it by running add_messages.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A state key declared without a reducer is overwritten by the most recent node that returns it.
questions.reason: Without a reducer, LangGraph's default channel simply keeps the last value written.

whys.a: Right: overwrite is the default behaviour, and R states the mechanism behind it.
whys.b: R is the explanation of A, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Add a reducer through Annotated[type, fn] whenever you need accumulation (messages, logs, counters). Be careful: in the same superstep, two writes to a plain key raise InvalidUpdateError.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: The add_messages reducer appends new messages instead of replacing the list.
questions.reason: A message whose id matches an existing message replaces that message.

whys.a: R is a detail about updates, not the reason appending happens, so a is wrong.
whys.b: Both are true: append is the general rule, replace-by-id is an extra feature that powers edits and RemoveMessage.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Both behaviours matter: the append builds the chat history, and replace-by-id lets a node correct a message or the framework update a streamed one.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A routing function passed to add_conditional_edges returns the name of the next node (or END).
questions.reason: The routing function must write the chosen route into the state, otherwise LangGraph cannot follow it.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true; R is false: the function only reads state and returns a name, and I ran graphs that never store the route.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Routers should be pure functions of state. If you want to update state and route in one step, return Command(update=..., goto=...) from a node.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Two nodes running in the same superstep can safely write a plain str state key without any reducer.
questions.reason: A reducer is the function that LangGraph uses to combine several updates to the same key.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError ('Can receive only one value per step'); R is true and is the fix.

questions.explanation: Parallel branches need reducers on any shared key, or branches should write to separate keys. I ran the failing case to see the error message.

questions.prompt: Match each LangGraph API with what it does.

right.text: Registers a function as a named step
Always moves from a to b
Chooses the next node from the function's return value
Lets a node change state and pick the next node together
Produces the runnable graph, optionally with persistence

questions.explanation: Threads are chosen at invoke time with config['configurable']['thread_id'], not by any of these builder calls.

questions.prompt: Complete the vocabulary of a LangGraph graph.
questions.text: The graph is built from a {1} schema, each node returns a partial {2}, and a {3} merges several writes to the same key.
questions.explanation: Nodes return only the keys they change. The schema can be a TypedDict, dataclass or Pydantic model.

questions.prompt: Complete the routing sentence for a tool path versus a text-to-SQL path.
questions.text: The function given to add_conditional_edges returns the {1} of the next node, and returning {2} finishes the run.
questions.explanation: A path map such as {'sql': 'sql_node', 'tool': 'tool_node'} lets the function return short labels instead of node names.

questions.prompt: Write a TypedDict State for LangGraph with a chat history key messages that appends via add_messages, and an integer key tokens_used that sums updates with operator.add.
questions.explanation: A bare add import (from operator import add) is equally valid. list[AnyMessage] is a common stricter type. MessagesState is a ready-made class that already contains the messages key.
questions.starter:
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages

questions.prompt: Variables State, classify, run_tool, run_sql and pick (returns 'sql' or 'tool') already exist. Build a StateGraph(State): nodes classify, tool and sql (functions run_tool, run_sql), START -> classify, a conditional edge from classify using pick with a path map to tool and sql, both ending at END, and compile it into app.

checks.label: conditional edges from classify with pick
tool and sql edges to END

questions.model:
g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("classify", classify)
g.add_node("tool", run_tool)
g.add_node("sql", run_sql)
g.add_edge(START, "classify")
g.add_conditional_edges("classify", pick, {"tool": "tool", "sql": "sql"})
g.add_edge("tool", END)
g.add_edge("sql", END)
app = g.compile()
questions.explanation: A list of names instead of the path map also works. add_edge(START, ...) and set_entry_point are equivalent for the entry. Chained add_node calls are fine too.

questions.prompt: Write a node classify(state) that returns a Command: if 'revenue' is in state['q'] it updates route to 'sql' and goes to the node 'sql_node', otherwise it updates route to 'tool' and goes to 'tool_node'.
questions.explanation: I ran a Command-based node. Annotate the return type with Command[Literal[...]] so graph drawing shows the possible destinations. An if/else with a single return also passes if both goto values appear.

questions.prompt: In a text-to-SQL branch, where should the check that generated SQL is a single read-only SELECT on allow-listed tables live?

options.text: In its own node between generation and execution, with a conditional edge back to regenerate on failure.
options.why: Right: an explicit step is testable, traceable and can loop back with the error.

options.text: Only in the system prompt, by telling the model never to write anything but SELECT statements.
options.why: A prompt is a request, not an enforcement; injected text can override it.

options.text: Nowhere in the graph, because the read-only database user will refuse anything unsafe in any case anyway.
options.why: A read-only DB role is necessary but it does not stop heavy queries or data from forbidden tables.

options.text: Inside the response node, after the query has executed and the rows were already read back.
options.why: Validation after execution is too late: the query has already run.

questions.explanation: Defence in depth: validate in code (parse, allow-list), run as a read-only role with a statement timeout and row limit, and keep the validator as a separate node so failures route back or to a human.

questions.prompt: Which statements about building a LangGraph graph are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nodes return only the state keys they change, not the whole state.
options.why: True: updates are partial and merged by reducers.

options.text: A graph must be compiled before you can call invoke or stream.
A node that returns None leaves the state unchanged.
options.why: True: I ran such a node and the state was untouched.

options.text: Every node must return a full copy of the state dictionary.
options.why: False: returning only changes is the norm.

options.text: A Pydantic BaseModel cannot be used as the state schema.
options.why: False: TypedDict, dataclass and Pydantic models are supported.

questions.explanation: Remember: schema, nodes, edges, compile, invoke with config. The state schema is the contract between nodes.

questions.prompt: In LangGraph, Annotated[list, add_messages] is the only way to keep a chat history in state.

options.why: Not true: a custom reducer such as operator.add on a list also works.
Right: add_messages is convenient (ids, replace, RemoveMessage), but any list with a reducer can hold history.

questions.explanation: add_messages adds message-aware merging. A plain Annotated[list, operator.add] only appends and cannot replace or delete by id.

questions.prompt: You find tutorial code using langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent. In LangGraph and LangChain 1.x, what is the status of that function?

options.text: Deprecated in favour of langchain.agents.create_agent, which takes system_prompt.
options.why: Right: the v1 migration guide points to create_agent as the successor.

options.text: It was removed together with StateGraph, so every agent must now be written by hand as nodes.
options.why: StateGraph is the core API of LangGraph 1.x and was not removed.

options.text: It still is the only prebuilt agent, and create_agent exists only for the JavaScript library.
options.why: create_agent exists for Python as well, in the langchain package.

options.text: It now requires a checkpointer, because agents without persistence are no longer supported.
options.why: A checkpointer is optional for agents, as for any compiled graph.

questions.explanation: Knowing the prebuilt is a ReAct-style loop (model node, tools node, conditional edge) matters more than the name; you can always build the same loop by hand with StateGraph.
